title: How can the two diagonals alone build a rhombus?
description: The longer diagonal is drawn first and cut at its midpoint. The shorter diagonal is drawn at a right angle through that midpoint, and joining the four ends gives the rhombus. Four matching triangles at the crossing check that all sides are equal.
teaching_notes: One idea: the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at a right angle, so the second diagonal is drawn at ninety degrees through the midpoint of the first. Watch for students who cross the diagonals at a slant or off the midpoint.

source: Figure it Out (parallelograms and rhombuses, question 3)
video_script.why: The child uses the fact that the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at a right angle to construct the rhombus from its diagonals.
video_script.substitution: the book's question with diagonals 4 cm and 5 cm
video_script.anchor: a segment AC of 5 cm with a line at right angles through its midpoint O, and B and D 2 cm from O on either side
video_script.payoff_line: Eigh B C D is the required rhombus

final_answer.value: ABCD, with diagonals 5 cm and 4 cm bisecting each other at right angles, is the rhombus
final_answer.spoken: A B C D is the rhombus, with diagonals of five and four centimetres bisecting each other at right angles

never_show: the diagonals crossing at a slant
maths_rules: the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at 90 degrees
AC = 5 cm, so AO = OC = 5 / 2 = 2.5 cm
BD = 4 cm, so OB = OD = 4 / 2 = 2 cm, drawn at 90 degrees to AC through O
the four triangles at O have legs 2.5 cm and 2 cm with a right angle between them, so they are congruent by SAS and AB = BC = CD = DA
all four sides are equal, so ABCD is a rhombus
